title: Tyson Foods Cuts Profit Outlook as Beef Losses Hit $142 Million in a Quarter
excerpt: America’s largest meat processor warns that soaring cattle costs will push full-year beef losses past $500 million, as a 75-year low in the U.S. herd reshapes protein markets.
body:
• Tyson Foods posted a $142 million loss in its beef division for fiscal Q3, with cattle costs climbing $575 million year-over-year, as record U.S. beef prices squeeze both meatpackers and consumers
  • The company widened its full-year beef loss forecast to $500–$650 million, up from $300–$500 million, while lowering overall profit guidance
  • A U.S. cattle shortage — with the herd at a 75-year low — has driven record retail beef prices, pushing American consumers toward cheaper chicken and pork
  • The reopening of the Mexican border for cattle imports may take a year to produce measurable relief for meatpackers

Tyson Foods, America’s largest meat processor, lowered its annual profit outlook on Monday after soaring cattle costs inflicted another heavy quarter of losses on its beef business — a result that underscores how a structural shortage in the U.S. cattle supply is reshaping the American protein market.

For the three months ended June 27, Tyson reported an adjusted profit of 99 cents per share, narrowly beating Wall Street’s expectation of 98 cents. But total sales were flat at $13.87 billion, missing analyst forecasts, as the beef segment continued its steep decline.

Beef Losses Deepen

Tyson’s beef division posted a $142 million operating loss for the fiscal third quarter. Beef sales prices rose almost 12% year-over-year, but volumes plunged 16% as record retail prices pushed consumers away from steaks and roasts. The company’s cattle costs climbed by $575 million compared with a year earlier.

For fiscal 2026, Tyson now expects an adjusted operating loss of $500 million to $650 million in beef, a sharp deterioration from its prior forecast of $300 million to $500 million.

“Beef hasn’t performed the way we expected, and we’re not pretending otherwise.”

— Donnie King, CEO, Tyson Foods

The Cattle Cycle Squeeze

The root cause is a multi-year drought that devastated U.S. pastures and forced ranchers to cull herds. The U.S. cattle herd shrank to a 75-year low as of January 2026, according to the Department of Agriculture. With fewer animals to buy, meatpackers face ballooning livestock costs that they cannot fully pass on through higher selling prices without destroying demand.

Tyson — which processes roughly one of every five pounds of chicken, beef and pork sold in the United States — has already closed a major beef plant in Lexington, Nebraska, that once employed 3,200 workers, and reduced operations at another facility in Amarillo, Texas.

Chicken Keeps Tyson Afloat

The company’s chicken business has become its financial anchor. Strong demand for nuggets, breasts and frozen products, combined with cheap livestock feed, has kept profits stable. But an industry-wide chicken glut over the past few months eroded wholesale values by 45% during the quarter.

CEO Donnie King argued Tyson is better insulated than competitors because most of its chicken volume feeds directly into Tyson-branded retail products rather than being sold at lower wholesale prices. “Industrywide chicken oversupply is a commodity-market dynamic,” King said. “This is not us.”

Mexico Border May Offer Relief — Eventually

The Agriculture Department said last month it will lift a more than yearlong ban on Mexican cattle imports, which historically make up about 5% of beef processed in U.S. facilities. Young calves are expected to begin crossing the border at the end of August, but Tyson executives cautioned it will take about a year before the company sees any financial benefit as cattle need months of fattening before slaughter.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian Americans, the beef-price surge is part of a broader food inflation picture that has strained household budgets. Chicken and pork — proteins more commonly consumed in Indian-American kitchens — have remained relatively affordable, but the cascading effects on restaurant prices, grocery bills and food-service stocks ripple through portfolios and daily spending alike. Tyson’s results also signal that the U.S. food-price relief consumers are hoping for may still be months away.

Looking Ahead

Tyson lowered its full-year adjusted operating income forecast to $2.1–$2.3 billion from $2.2–$2.4 billion and narrowed its sales growth outlook to 2.5–3.5%. The company said fiscal 2027 is likely to look much like 2026, with the cattle cycle unlikely to turn before then. Shares rose 2.4% on the day, suggesting investors had already priced in the beef pain and were encouraged by management’s candour.
